exercises.blurbEn: A headline in compressed newspaper Korean, and four readings of it — three of which are what taking one word literally looks like.
exercises.instructionKo: 다음 신문 기사의 제목을 가장 잘 설명한 것을 고르십시오.
exercises.instructionEn: Choose the sentence that best explains the newspaper headline.
exercises.noteEn:
A headline drops its particles and its verb endings, so every word left carries more than usual and can usually be read two ways. The options are not four summaries — they are four readings, and the wrong ones are wrong in a small number of repeating shapes.

Seven shapes, across the ten questions here.

1. A figurative word taken at face value. 출구 as a door, 관리 as a job, 찬물 as a temperature, 꿀 as honey.
2. A description turned into a recommendation. -어야 한다 and 필요가 있다 in an option are the tell; a headline advises nobody.
3. An addition read as a comparison. Enjoying food with the eyes *as well* is not taste mattering less.
4. The subject quietly swapped, so a problem the headline gave to one party is handed to another.
5. A time or quantity expression read as something adjacent. N 만에 is a point measured back to the last occurrence; N 동안 is the whole stretch. Swap them and the sentence still reads well and claims something else.
6. The headline reversed in its own vocabulary. Every word of the option comes from the headline and the claim is the opposite one. Reusing the words is what makes it look like a summary.
7. The claim narrowed by a condition the headline never set. -아/어야, 자기 전에. Not advice and no new fact, so it slips past both of those checks — what it changes is how much the headline claims.

And three things to do before weighing any of them.

Find the words that can be read two ways and settle those first. Check who the headline says is doing what. And read past whatever all four options share — that part is there to make them look alike, not to be the question.

Two shapes of headline are worth knowing on sight. A quotation with a verdict attached — "…" plus 착각, 논란, 오해 — is not passing the quote on; the verdict is the news, and the answer will be about the belief rather than about what the belief is about. And quotation marks anywhere mark something not to be read as ordinary text: a title, a name, a word quoted for its sound. Whatever is inside them has stopped meaning what its parts mean.

items.phraseKo: 썰렁한 재래시장, 배달로 출구 모색

lines.ko: 썰렁한 재래시장, 배달로 출구 모색

choices.ko: 재래시장은 출입구가 여러 곳에 있어 찾기가 쉽지 않다.
날씨가 추워지자 재래시장을 직접 찾는 손님들이 줄었다.
재래시장에서 배달 서비스를 통해 경기 회복의 노력을 하고 있다.
재래시장에서 상품을 구매한 후 배달을 원하는 사람들이 많아졌다.

items.en: Deserted traditional markets seek a way out through delivery — the markets are trying to bring trade back with a delivery service.
items.why:
Two words in the headline can each be read two ways, and every wrong option is one of them taken at face value.

썰렁하다 is the first. Day to day it means chilly, but said of a shop or a street it means empty — nobody in it, nothing selling. A market headline wants that second sense, and option 2 is exactly what choosing the first one looks like: a perfectly good Korean sentence about the weather that says nothing at all about the other half of the headline.

출구 is the second. On a door it is the way out of a building; in 출구를 모색하다 it is the way out of trouble, and 모색 is casting about for one. Option 1 reads it as a door and ends up describing the floor plan.

That leaves who is doing the seeking. The headline's subject is the market, so the market is the one turning to delivery. Option 4 keeps every word and swaps the actor — customers wanting delivery is a different story, and swapping who acts is one of the commonest ways this question type is got wrong. Option 3 is the only reading that keeps the market as the agent and takes both hinge words figuratively: 경기 회복의 노력 is 출구 모색 said plainly.
items.grammar: Headline Korean. A Sino-Korean noun stands in for its verb — 모색 does the work of 모색하고 있다 — and the comma does the work of a subject marker. N(으)로 marks the means: 배달로 = by way of delivery. In the options, N을/를 통해 is the same idea spelled out, and -자 in 추워지자 means 'as soon as / once', linking a change to what followed it. 기사 on its own is the article; 제목 is its title, and the two together are 신문 기사 제목, the name of this question type.

items.phraseKo: 눈으로 먹고 귀로 맛보는 시대, 요리 프로그램 천국!

lines.ko: 눈으로 먹고 귀로 맛보는 시대, 요리 프로그램 천국!

choices.ko: 음식을 먹을 때에는 눈과 귀로도 즐겨야 한다.
요즘 요리에 관련된 텔레비전 프로그램이 아주 많다.
이제는 음식의 맛보다 모양이나 색깔이 더 중요해졌다.
텔레비전에서는 실제 요리보다 사진이나 그림을 더 많이 보여준다.

items.en: An age of eating with the eyes and tasting with the ears — a paradise of cooking programmes. Meaning: there are a great many cooking programmes on television now.
items.why:
천국 is the hinge, and it is not a place. 요리 프로그램 천국 says there are so many cooking programmes that the country is awash with them, and option 2 is that said in plain words: 아주 많다.

The first half describes rather than instructs. 눈으로 먹고 귀로 맛보는 시대 says this is the age we are in — food consumed through pictures and sound. Option 1 turns it into 즐겨야 한다, an obligation nobody in the headline is under. A headline reports a state of affairs; it does not tell the reader what to do.

Option 3 goes further than the words allow. Enjoying food with the eyes and ears *as well* says nothing about taste mattering less — the headline adds senses, it does not rank them. Reading a comparison into an addition is the commonest way to overshoot on this question type.

Option 4 reverses the second half outright. A cooking-programme paradise is the opposite of television showing pictures instead of cooking.
items.grammar: N(으)로 marks the instrument: 눈으로, 귀로 — with the eyes, with the ears. -는 시대 makes a whole clause modify 시대, so 눈으로 먹고 귀로 맛보는 all describes the era rather than being separate statements. And the headline ends on a bare noun where a verb belongs: 천국! stands in for 천국이다, the same compression as 모색 for 모색하고 있다 in question 1.

items.phraseKo: 색조 화장품도 불티, 남자는 관리 중

lines.ko: 색조 화장품도 불티, 남자는 관리 중

choices.ko: 화장을 하는 등 외모를 가꾸는 남자들이 늘어났다.
남자를 위한 화장품도 다양하게 만들 필요가 있다.
화장품의 색을 만드는 일은 주로 남자들이 담당하고 있다.
사회적 지위가 높은 남자들이 외모에 관심을 많이 갖는다.

items.en: Colour cosmetics selling out too, and men are grooming. Meaning: more men are looking after their appearance, makeup included.
items.why:
Two words with two readings each, which by now is the shape of this question type rather than a coincidence.

불티 is a spark, and on its own says nothing about selling. It is the front half of 불티나다 — to go like sparks off a fire — which is what Korean says when stock clears as fast as it arrives. The headline keeps the spark and drops the verb. The particle 도 is doing the real work: colour cosmetics *as well*, not just the skincare a reader would already expect men to buy.

관리 중 is the second. 관리하다 is both to look after and to be in charge of, and 중 is in the middle of doing it. Of a person and their own face it is grooming; of a person and a task it is a job. Option 3 takes the second reading and builds a workplace out of it — men run the colour-making — and has to misread 색조 화장품 as "making colours" to get there at all.

Option 2 turns a report into a recommendation: 만들 필요가 있다 is advice, and a headline advises nobody. That is the same miss as option 1 in question 2.

Option 4 adds a fact the headline does not contain. 사회적 지위 appears nowhere in it — the headline says men, not men of a certain standing.

Which leaves 1, and it is both halves said plainly: cosmetics flying off shelves means men buying them, 관리 중 means grooming, and 늘어났다 is the trend that 도 was pointing at.
items.grammar: Headline compression twice in one line: 불티 stands in for 불티나게 팔린다 and 관리 중 for 관리하고 있다 — the third headline running to put a noun where the verb belongs. N도 is the particle carrying the news: 색조 화장품도 means these too, on top of what you would expect. And in option 1, -는 등 names one example among several: 화장을 하는 등 = by wearing makeup and so on.

items.phraseKo: 피서객은 '더위와의 전쟁', 피서지는 '쓰레기와의 전쟁'

lines.ko: 피서객은 '더위와의 전쟁', 피서지는 '쓰레기와의 전쟁'

choices.ko: 피서지에서는 많은 양의 쓰레기를 치우는 문제가 심각하다.
피서객들이 더위 속에서 쓰레기를 치우기 위해 애쓰고 있다.
피서지에 가도 날씨가 너무 덥기 때문에 편하게 쉴 수 없다.
피서객들이 쓰레기 문제로 인해 여러 가지로 불편을 겪고 있다.

items.en: For holidaymakers a war with the heat, for the resorts a war with the rubbish. Meaning: clearing the volume of litter left behind has become a serious problem where people go to escape the summer.
items.why:
This one is not a word with two readings. It is a pairing, and the pairing is the whole question.

The headline sets two subjects against two different enemies: 피서객 against the heat, 피서지 against the rubbish. Two of the wrong options simply swap them. Option 2 has the holidaymakers clearing litter in the heat, option 4 has them inconvenienced by the litter — both hand 피서객 a problem the headline gave to the resort. Every word in them is a word from the headline, which is exactly what makes them attractive.

Option 3 takes only the first half and then adds to it. 편하게 쉴 수 없다 is a conclusion about resting that the headline never draws; it says holidaymakers are fighting the heat, not that the trip is ruined.

That leaves 1, which is the second half decoded. 전쟁 is the metaphor to unpack: a headline calls something a war when it is a problem nobody is winning, and 심각하다 is that said plainly. The 많은 양 is where the war comes from.

Worth noticing which half the answer comes from. Both halves are true, and the one the options are built around is the second — the newsworthy one. A headline in two halves does not promise the answer covers both.
items.grammar:
N와/과의 전쟁 — a war *with* N. 와/과 marks who the fight is against, and 의 turns the whole thing into something that can sit as a noun in a headline, where a verb would otherwise be needed. The same compression as 모색, 천국 and 불티 in the questions before it.

In the options: -기 위해 states a purpose (치우기 위해 = in order to clear), and N(으)로 인해 states a cause in the formal register the papers use (쓰레기 문제로 인해 = owing to the rubbish problem).

items.phraseKo: 저축률 24년 만에 바닥으로, 젊은층도 저축 무관심!

lines.ko: 저축률 24년 만에 바닥으로, 젊은층도 저축 무관심!

choices.ko: 24년 동안 저축률이 계속 오르지 않고 있다.
젊은 때 저축을 시작해서 24년 정도 하는 게 좋다.
저축률이 한 번 떨어졌다 올라가는 데 24년이 걸린다.
젊은층을 비롯해서 저축률이 24년 만에 가장 낮게 나타났다.

items.en: The savings rate has hit rock bottom for the first time in 24 years, and even the young are indifferent to saving. Meaning: the savings rate, the young included, has come out at its lowest in 24 years.
items.why:
The hinge here is not a metaphor. It is a time expression, and three of the four options get it wrong in three different ways.

N 만에 means after an interval of N — in practice, for the first time in N years, measured from the last time it happened. It does not mean *during* N years, which is N 동안, and option 1 is that one substitution and nothing else: 24년 동안 … 오르지 않고 있다 claims the rate has failed to rise for twenty-four years running. That is a far stronger statement than the headline makes. The headline says only that today's figure is the lowest since twenty-four years ago; about the twenty-three years in between it says nothing at all.

Option 3 turns the interval into a mechanism — twenty-four years for the rate to fall and climb back. Nothing in the headline is about recovery; it reports a floor, not a cycle.

Option 2 turns it into advice on how long to save for, which misreads 만에 and is also the recommendation shape that keeps turning up in this question type.

That leaves 4, which is the easy half done right. 바닥 is rock bottom and 가장 낮게 is that said plainly; 만에 survives intact; and 젊은층도 becomes 젊은층을 비롯해서 — the 도 saying the young are part of the fall, not a separate story beside it.
items.grammar:
N 만에 against N 동안 is the whole question. 24년 만에 = for the first time in 24 years, measured from the last occurrence; 24년 동안 = throughout 24 years. One names a point, the other a stretch, and swapping them changes what is being claimed rather than how it is worded.

N을/를 비롯해서 = including N, and N first among them, which is the work 도 does in 젊은층도. And 바닥으로 is a bare noun plus 으로 where a verb belongs: the headline standing in for 바닥으로 떨어졌다, the same compression as 모색, 천국, 불티 and 관리 중 before it.

items.phraseKo: 여름철 음식 보관, 냉장고만 믿어서는 낭패!

lines.ko: 여름철 음식 보관, 냉장고만 믿어서는 낭패!

choices.ko: 먹던 음식을 냉장고에 넣는 것은 좋지 않다.
여름에는 모든 음식을 냉장고에 보관해야 한다.
여름에는 냉장고 안의 음식도 안심하고 먹을 수 없다.
여름철에 음식을 보관하려면 특별한 냉장고를 마련해야 한다.

items.en: Storing food in summer: trusting the fridge and nothing else is asking for trouble. Meaning: in summer even the food inside the fridge cannot be eaten with confidence.
items.why:
The whole question is one particle. Cover 만 and the headline says something close to the opposite.

냉장고만 믿어서는 낭패 is: rely on the fridge *alone* and you will come unstuck. It does not say the fridge is useless, and it does not say to use it more. It says the fridge is not enough by itself — so the food inside one is not automatically safe.

Option 2 is that reversed while keeping every word. 여름, 음식, 냉장고, 보관 are all from the headline, and 모든 음식을 냉장고에 보관해야 한다 tells you to trust the fridge more, which is the one instruction the headline is warning against. Reusing the vocabulary is what makes it look right; it is also all it has.

Option 4 recommends buying something. 특별한 냉장고 appears nowhere in the headline, and a headline saying the fridge is not enough is not selling a better fridge. Option 2 and option 4 are both -해야 한다 — that is four of the six questions so far where an option turns a report into advice.

Option 1 is the quieter trap: 먹던 음식을 냉장고에 넣는 것은 좋지 않다 is true as food safety goes, and 먹던 음식 is nowhere in the headline. It is a fact about the topic rather than a reading of the sentence — the same move as 사회적 지위 in question 3.

That leaves 3, and it is 만 unpacked. If the fridge alone is a 낭패, then 냉장고 안의 음식도 — the food inside it *too* — is not something you can eat 안심하고. The 도 is the same particle that carried the news in question 3: even this one, on top of what you already assumed.
items.grammar:
N만 = N and nothing besides. It is the load-bearing word here, and it is one syllable: 냉장고를 믿어서는 낭패 would be "trusting fridges is a disaster", while 냉장고만 믿어서는 낭패 is "trusting only fridges is". The exam puts the whole question on that difference.

V-아/어서는 introduces a course of action that ends badly, and what ends it is always negative — here 낭패. The full sentence is 믿어서는 낭패를 본다; the headline keeps the noun and drops the verb, which is now six headlines running to do it: 모색, 천국, 불티, 관리 중, 바닥으로, 낭패.

In the options: -던 (먹던 음식) is the one you were in the middle of eating, -(으)려면 (보관하려면) is if you intend to, and -아/어야 하다 is the recommendation shape worth being suspicious of. 믿다 is to trust, and 믿어서는 is that verb wearing the ending above. 두 동사도 함께: 보관하다 is to store and 마련하다 is to get hold of — the second is what options 2 and 4 are really asking you to do, and neither is what the headline says.

items.phraseKo: 정부의 집값 잡기, 서민 경제에 찬물 끼얹는 중

lines.ko: 정부의 집값 잡기, 서민 경제에 찬물 끼얹는 중

choices.ko: 정부의 부동산 정책이 서민 경제에 악영향을 미치고 있다.
정부의 부동산 정책 때문에 서민 물가가 많이 떨어지고 있다.
정부의 부동산 정책을 시민들이 아주 냉정하게 평가하고 있다.
정부의 부동산 정책이 시민들의 마음을 시원하게 해 주고 있다.

items.en: The government's drive to rein in house prices is pouring cold water on ordinary households. Meaning: the policy is doing harm to the everyday economy.
items.why:
Start with what the four options have in common, because it is not the question. All four open with 정부의 부동산 정책 — the standard paraphrase of 정부의 집값 잡기. Shared wording cannot separate them, so the whole question is in what comes after it, and what comes after it is four readings of 찬물 끼얹는 중.

찬물을 끼얹다 is an idiom: to throw cold water over something that was going well and spoil it. It is never neutral and never good.

Two of the options take the cold literally, and go opposite ways with it. Option 3 hears 찬 and arrives at 냉정하게, cool-headed — and while it is there it also swaps who acts on whom: in the headline the policy chills the economy, in option 3 the citizens coolly appraise the policy. Option 4 hears the same cold and arrives at 시원하게, refreshing, which flips the sentence from harm to relief while leaving every other word alone — the reversal from question 6, done through a feeling rather than through vocabulary.

Option 2 changes one noun. 집값 is house prices; 물가 is what everything costs. They are not the same thing, and a headline saying the drive is chilling household budgets is not saying those budgets got cheaper. Falling 물가 would be the good news the idiom rules out.

That leaves 1, which is the idiom in plain words: 악영향을 미치고 있다, it is having a bad effect. Cold water on something, said without the picture.
items.grammar:
찬물을 끼얹다 is fixed: literally to pour cold water over, used only of spoiling a good mood or a good run. Learn it whole — the parts do not add up to the meaning, which is exactly what options 3 and 4 are built on.

-는 중 is in the middle of doing, the same 중 as 관리 중 in question 3. And 잡기 is 잡다 with -기, the ending that turns a verb into something a headline can put a possessive in front of: 정부의 집값 잡기. Seven headlines, seven nouns standing where a verb belongs — 모색, 천국, 불티, 관리 중, 바닥으로, 낭패, 잡기.

In the options: 영향을 미치다 is the set phrase for having an effect (악영향 is the bad kind), N 때문에 gives a cause, and -게 하다 makes something turn out a certain way — 시원하게 해 주다, to leave someone feeling refreshed. Worth splitting the paraphrase into its parts: 부동산 is property, 정책 is a policy, and 경제 is an economy — so 부동산 정책 and 서민 경제 are each two ordinary words rather than one hard one.

items.phraseKo: "우리 개는 안 물어요." 주인들의 흔한 착각

lines.ko: "우리 개는 안 물어요." 주인들의 흔한 착각

choices.ko: 자신의 반려견에게 물리는 사람들이 늘고 있다.
개를 키우기 전에 개의 특성에 대해서 알아봐야 한다.
한번 사람을 문 적이 있는 개는 다시 사람을 물 수 있다.
자신의 반려견은 물지 않는다고 확신하는 것은 잘못된 것이다.

items.en: "Our dog doesn’t bite." — the mistake owners keep making. Meaning: being sure your own dog will never bite is itself the error.
items.why:
This headline is built differently from the seven before it. It is a quotation followed by a verdict on the quotation: someone says 우리 개는 안 물어요, and the paper labels that 흔한 착각. A headline that quotes a line and then names it a 착각 is not passing the line on — it is correcting it. The label is the news, and if you read past 착각 the headline appears to be saying dogs do not bite.

Now look at what the second half is grammatically about. Not dogs. 착각 is a thought, and the headline is about what owners believe. Three of the four options are about dogs: who gets bitten, what to research, which dogs bite twice. Only one is about the belief, and that is 4 — 확신하는 것은 잘못된 것이다, being certain is the thing that is wrong. It even keeps the quotation, turning the spoken 안 물어요 into the written 물지 않는다.

Option 1 makes it a statistic. 늘고 있다 counts something, and the headline counts nothing; it reports a mistake, not a trend.

Option 2 is advice again — 알아봐야 한다. That is the fifth time in eight questions that an option has turned a report into a recommendation, and it has been wrong every time.

Option 3 is the quiet one, and it is true: a dog that has bitten once may bite again. But it is about a different set of dogs entirely. The headline is about owners whose dogs have never bitten anyone — that is precisely why they are sure. A statement can be true about the subject and still not be a reading of the sentence.
items.grammar:
착각 carries the whole headline and it is a bare noun: 주인들의 흔한 착각, with 착각이다 or 착각하고 있다 left off. Eight headlines, eight nouns standing where a verb belongs — 모색, 천국, 불티, 관리 중, 바닥으로, 낭패, 잡기, 착각.

The two negatives are worth putting side by side, because this question has both. 안 물어요 is the short negative, which is what people say out loud; 물지 않는다 is the long one, which is what a written option uses. Same claim, two registers, and the shift from one to the other is a sign an option is quoting the headline back at you.

물다 is to bite and 물리다 is to be bitten — the passive, which is why option 1 has 물리는 사람들, people getting bitten. And -다고 확신하다 is to be certain that: an indirect quotation with the verb of believing attached to it. 키우다 is to keep an animal — the verb behind 키우기 전에.

items.phraseKo: 꿀잠 자게 해 주는 바나나, 불안감도 '사르르'

lines.ko: 꿀잠 자게 해 주는 바나나, 불안감도 '사르르'

choices.ko: 바나나를 꿀과 함께 먹으면 잠을 푹 잘 수 있다.
바나나는 자기 전에 먹어야 불안감에도 효과가 있다.
바나나는 숙면에도 도움이 될뿐더러 불안감도 없애 준다
바나나를 먹을 때 속이 불편한 사람은 꿀과 함께 먹는 게 좋다.

items.en: Bananas that give you a deep night’s sleep — and anxiety melts away too. Meaning: bananas not only help you sleep soundly, they also take anxiety away.
items.why:
꿀잠 is 꿀 and 잠 stuck together, and it means a deep, sweet night’s sleep. There is no honey in it. It is the same trick as 찬물 in question 7, down to the count: two of the four options read the first syllable literally and put honey on the plate. Option 1 has you eat the banana 꿀과 함께, option 4 has people with delicate stomachs do the same. Neither is a reading of the headline; both are a reading of one syllable.

Now the 도, because it is what holds the headline together. 불안감도 사르르 means anxiety melts away *as well* — on top of the sleep. So the headline makes two claims and links them, and an option that keeps only one of them has dropped the link. Option 1 keeps the sleep and loses the anxiety entirely.

Worth putting beside question 4, which had a two-part headline whose answer came from one half only. The difference is the 도. There the two halves had different subjects — holidaymakers against the heat, resorts against the rubbish — two separate facts, and an option could take either. Here 도 stacks the second claim on the first about the same subject, so both have to survive.

Option 2 keeps both topics and then narrows the claim: 자기 전에 먹어야 — only if you eat them before bed. The headline sets no such condition, and 먹어야 quietly demotes the sleep benefit into a precondition for the anxiety one, when the headline offers them side by side.

That leaves 3, which is both halves in plain words and keeps the stacking: 숙면에도 도움이 될뿐더러 불안감도 없애 준다. -(으)ㄹ뿐더러 is "not only that, but also" — it is what 도 looks like when a sentence has to write it out.
items.grammar:
꿀잠 = 꿀 + 잠. 꿀 in front of a noun is a colloquial intensifier meaning the good kind: 꿀팁 is a great tip, 꿀템 a great buy. None of them involve honey, and that is the whole of options 1 and 4.

사르르 is 의태어 — a word that imitates a manner rather than a sound, here the way something dissolves quietly (사르르 녹다, 사르르 사라지다). The headline puts it in quotation marks and leaves the verb off: ninth headline, ninth word standing where a verb belongs.

-게 해 주다: 꿀잠 자게 해 주는 바나나 = bananas that let you sleep deeply. -(으)ㄹ뿐더러 is the formal "not only … but also". And -아/어야 states a condition, not advice — 먹어야 효과가 있다 is "it only works if you eat them", which is a different sort of wrong answer from 먹어야 한다. 자다 is to sleep, which is the verb inside both 꿀잠 자게 and 자기 전에.

items.phraseKo: 서점가는 지금 '행복 열차' 앓이... 한 달 새 10만 부나 팔려

lines.ko: 서점가는 지금 '행복 열차' 앓이... 한 달 새 10만 부나 팔려

choices.ko: 현재 '행복 열차'라는 책이 큰 인기를 얻고 있다.
'행복 열차'라는 책이 서점에서 이번 달까지만 판매된다.
서점에 가면 '행복 열차'라는 책을 읽고 있는 사람들이 많다.

items.en: The book trade has 'Happiness Train' fever — a hundred thousand copies in a single month. Meaning: the book called 'Happiness Train' is hugely popular right now.
items.why:
Three things to settle, and the headline hands you all three.

First the quotation marks. '행복 열차' is in quotes, and 서점가 says what world we are in: the book trade. So it is a title, and the words inside a title are not there to be read for their meaning. Option 2 reads them anyway and puts a real train on real rails — 열차가 운행을 시작했다. This is the second question running where quotation marks are the signal: question 9 put 사르르 in them to mark a word standing in for a verb. One mark, two jobs, and both times the job is do not read this as ordinary running text.

Worth noticing what the other three options do with it. All of them say 책. They agree because 서점가 already settled it, and option 2 is the one that ignored a context word the headline gave away for free. That is the tell — not that three options outvote one, but that one of them contradicts something already fixed.

Second, 앓이. It comes from 앓다, to be ill, and as an ending it turns whatever it attaches to into a craze for that thing. 서점가는 지금 '행복 열차' 앓이 = the book trade has come down with it. Nobody is ill, and nobody is standing in a shop. Option 4 invents a symptom — people reading on the premises — and to get there it swaps 서점가, the trade, for 서점, a shop you can walk into, and 팔리다, sold, for 읽다, being read. The headline counts sales.

Third, 한 달 새 10만 부나 팔려. The 나 is the whole point of the number: it means as many as, and it exists to say the figure is larger than you would expect. That is the evidence for the craze. Option 3 turns the month back to front. 한 달 새 is a month that has already gone by; 이번 달까지만 판매된다 is a deadline still ahead. The word doing the damage is 만 — the same particle that decided question 6, this time narrowing rather than excluding.

Which leaves 1, and it is the whole headline in five words: 큰 인기를 얻고 있다.
items.grammar:
-앓이 is productive: 앓다 (to be ill) gives 앓이, and it attaches to whatever people are obsessed with — 아이돌 앓이, 몸살앓이. In a headline it is always a craze, never a diagnosis.

N(이)라는 = called N. '행복 열차'라는 책 is a book called Happiness Train, and it is how three of the four options tell you what kind of thing they are talking about. 이름의 in option 2 does the same job for the train it invented.

새 is 사이 worn short: 한 달 새 = 한 달 사이, in the space of a month. And N(이)나 after a quantity means as many as — 10만 부나 팔려 — which is a different 나 from the one meaning or.

팔려 is 팔리다 clipped where a headline would rather stop than conjugate: tenth headline, tenth verb either cut short or replaced by a noun.

items.phraseKo: TV 프로그램 방영 효과 '톡톡', 인주시는 관광객 물결

lines.ko: TV 프로그램 방영 효과 '톡톡', 인주시는 관광객 물결

choices.ko: TV 프로그램 제작자들이 관광객을 촬영하러 인주시로 모여들었다.
인주시가 TV 프로그램에 나온 덕분에 많은 관광객이 방문하고 있다.
인주시가 관광객 유치를 위해 TV 프로그램 홍보 방송을 준비하고 있다.
TV 프로그램 방송 후에 관광객이 증가해 인주시에 여러 문제가 발생했다.

items.en: A television programme has paid off handsomely, and Inju City is awash with tourists.
items.why:
방영 효과 톡톡 is the broadcast paying off, and 관광객 물결 is what it paid off in — a wave of visitors. So the headline says one thing: being on television has filled Inju with tourists. ② says exactly that, and 덕분에 is the causal word 톡톡 is implying.

① keeps every noun and reverses the direction of travel. The headline has tourists arriving in Inju; ① has programme-makers arriving to film the tourists. That is the subject quietly swapped, the fourth of the shapes this type keeps using, and reusing the vocabulary is what makes it read like a summary.

③ turns a result into a plan. 준비하고 있다 means the broadcast has not gone out yet, and 방영 효과 means it has and the effect is already being felt. A headline reporting an effect is never reporting a preparation.

④ imports a downside from nowhere. 물결 is a wave of visitors and 톡톡 is a pleased word; the headline is reporting a success. 여러 문제가 발생했다 is a claim about consequences that none of these seven words makes.
items.grammar:
톡톡히 is the word to know. 효과를 톡톡히 보다 is to get a solid benefit out of something, and a headline clipping it to 톡톡 inside quotation marks is quoting the adverb rather than a sound. Quotation marks in a headline always mark something not to be read as ordinary text.

물결 is a wave, and Korean uses it for any surge of people or of feeling: 관광객 물결, 시위 물결. It is a noun, so the headline ends without a verb — normal in this register and part of why the options have to supply one.

덕분에 credits a good outcome to something, 때문에 is neutral and 탓에 blames. Only 덕분에 fits a headline pleased about what happened.

유치 is attracting something to your area — 관광객 유치, 기업 유치, 올림픽 유치. It is not the 유치하다 that means childish, which is a different word entirely.

items.phraseKo: 김수미 선수 시상대에 올라, 펜싱 종목 메달 가뭄 끝

lines.ko: 김수미 선수 시상대에 올라, 펜싱 종목 메달 가뭄 끝

choices.ko: 김 선수가 펜싱 대표팀에서 메달을 목표로 열심히 훈련했다.
김 선수가 메달을 따면서 오랜만에 펜싱 종목에서 메달이 나왔다.
김 선수가 가장 많은 메달을 따며 펜싱 종목에서 신기록을 세웠다.
김 선수가 펜싱 종목에서 좋은 경기를 펼쳤지만 아쉽게 메달을 놓쳤다.

items.en: Kim Su-mi steps onto the podium, ending the medal drought in fencing.
items.why:
시상대에 올라 is stepping onto the winners' podium, so she took a medal. 메달 가뭄 끝 says the drought is over: fencing had gone a long time without one. ② carries both halves — she won a medal, and 오랜만에 a medal came in the fencing.

④ is the headline reversed in its own vocabulary, which is the sixth shape and the one worth checking hardest. 시상대에 오르다 and 메달을 놓쳤다 cannot both be true. Every word of the option comes from the headline and the claim is the opposite one.

③ overstates what a drought ending means. 가뭄 끝 is one medal after a long gap — the lowest bar there is — and 가장 많은 메달 with 신기록 is the highest. Nothing in the headline compares her with anyone.

① reports the preparation rather than the result. 훈련했다 is what happened before, and 메달을 목표로 puts the medal still ahead of her. The headline has her already on the podium.
items.grammar:
가뭄 is a drought of rain, and Korean lends it to any long absence of something wanted: 메달 가뭄, 골 가뭄, 일감 가뭄. 끝 after it is a noun, so the whole headline runs without a verb.

시상대에 오르다 takes 에, like 무대에 오르다 and 정상에 오르다. It is the standard way of saying someone placed, and it does not say which colour of medal.

따다 is what you do to a medal, a licence or a fruit — 메달을 따다, 자격증을 따다. Its opposite here is 놓치다, to let something slip, which takes the same object.

경기 in this paper means business conditions, and the 경기 in 좋은 경기를 펼치다 is the other one — a sporting contest. 경기를 펼치다 is to put on a performance, and it is entered here as a phrase so that the trade sense stays where it belongs.

오랜만에 is after a long interval, and it is one word: the 만에 inside it is not the N 만에 that measures back to a last occurrence.

items.phraseKo: 선 넘은 악성 댓글, 처벌은 여전히 솜방망이

lines.ko: 선 넘은 악성 댓글, 처벌은 여전히 솜방망이

choices.ko: 악의적인 댓글이 줄어든 만큼 처벌 수위를 낮추자는 의견이 제기됐다.
악의적인 댓글에 대한 처벌을 강화했으나 피해는 감소하지 않고 있다.
악의적인 댓글이 지나치게 심각해졌음에도 처벌 수위는 아직도 너무 낮다.
악의적인 댓글이 계속 이어지자 피해자들이 무거운 처벌을 요구하고 나섰다.

items.en: Malicious comments have gone past the line, and the punishment is still a slap on the wrist.
items.why:
Two halves pulling against each other. 선 넘은 악성 댓글 says the comments have gone past what is acceptable; 처벌은 여전히 솜방망이 says the penalty is still far too soft. The problem got worse and the punishment did not move. ③ says both.

솜방망이 is the whole question. A 방망이 is a club; one made of 솜 — cotton wool — hits nothing. 솜방망이 처벌 is the set phrase for a penalty too light to deter anyone, and once it is read as light rather than as an object, the headline's complaint is plain.

② has the punishment strengthened, which is what 여전히 rules out. 여전히 is not decoration: it says nothing has changed, so any option describing a change is wrong before its second half is read.

① reverses both halves at once — comments falling, penalties to be lowered — while using the headline's own nouns. 선 넘다 is an increase in the problem, not a decrease.

④ brings in people the headline never mentions. Victims stepping forward to demand heavier punishment is a plausible next article, and there is nothing in these eight words about victims or about anyone demanding anything. A headline complains here; it does not report a campaign.
items.grammar:
선(을) 넘다 is to cross the line, in the same figurative sense English has. The headline drops the particle, as headlines do, leaving 선 넘은 as a modifier on 댓글.

악성 and 악의적 are both malicious and the paper uses one in the headline and the other in every option. 악성 attaches straight to a noun — 악성 댓글, 악성 코드 — while 악의적 needs -인 before one.

여전히 is still, of a state that has not changed, and 아직도 is still, of something that ought to have finished by now. The headline uses the first and the answer uses the second, which is the swap that makes ③ a paraphrase rather than a repetition.

수위 is a water level, and 처벌 수위 borrows it for how severe a punishment is: 수위를 높이다, 수위를 낮추다. -(으)ㄴ 만큼 in ① measures one thing against another — to the extent that they have fallen.

-았/었음에도 is even though, built on the noun form -(으)ㅁ, and it belongs to writing. Its everyday twin is -았/었는데도.

exercises.instructionKo: ( )에 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르십시오.
exercises.instructionEn: Choose the expression that best fits the blank.
exercises.blurbEn: One sentence, one gap, and four endings on the same verb — so the answer is never in the vocabulary.
exercises.noteEn:
A sentence with a hole in it and four endings on the same verb. Because the verb never changes, no amount of vocabulary will settle it — the answer is always in the words around the blank.

Three things to read before the options.

Time words and the particles on them. 오전에는 … 지금은, with 은/는 on both, is a contrast being set up, and only some endings can hold one. 앞으로 fixes the direction of travel.

Whether the first clause is a fact or a supposition. Half the endings offered will be concessive or conditional, and those need a supposition. If two of the four mean the same thing, both are wrong — an exam does not offer two correct answers.

Who is speaking, and about whom. Several endings here are restricted by person: -더라 needs someone other than the speaker, -아/어야지 needs the speaker themselves, -(으)려고 needs the intender and the doer to be the same. A quotation mark or a name in front of the sentence can settle two options before you have weighed what any of them mean.

And read the end of the sentence before the options. -다니 needs a contrast in front of it. 대체적으로 with a completed past is asking for a hedged cause, not a supposition.

The endings that keep turning up in this slot: -더니 (I saw A, then B, and B surprises), -더라도 (even if A, still B), -아/어 가지고 (A, and so B), -는 대신에 (B in place of A), -아/어서인지 (perhaps because A), -는 한 (for as long as A holds), -게 하다 against -게 되다 (somebody made it happen, or it came about).

items.phraseKo: 오전에는 비가 많이 (   ) 지금은 날씨가 맑게 개었다.

lines.ko: 오전에는 비가 많이 {} 지금은 날씨가 맑게 개었다.

items.en: It rained hard in the morning, and now the sky has cleared. The ending has to carry a then and a now that disagree.
items.why:
All four options are the same verb. 오다 does not move; only the ending does, and that is what this question type is. So the sentence around the blank is the whole of the evidence — and the sentence gives you two time words, 오전에는 and 지금은, set against each other, with 은/는 on both marking the contrast.

One ending is built for exactly that. -더니 says: I saw A, and then B, and B is not what A led you to expect. 오전에는 비가 오더니 지금은 개었다 is its natural shape.

Option 2 is the concessive. -더라도 means even if, and what it concedes is hypothetical — it might rain, it might not. But 오전에는 pins the rain to a past morning as a fact, and 개었다 is a finished event rather than something that holds in spite of rain.

Option 3 is 와서 in its spoken clothes. -아/어 가지고 makes the first clause the cause of the second or the step before it, so the sentence would have to end with something the rain brought about. Clearing up is the opposite of what rain brings about.

Option 4 says the rain did not happen. -는 대신에 puts one thing in place of another, and 비가 많이 says plainly that it did.

Which leaves 1. Worth noticing how little Korean you had to read: the two time markers decided it, and the vocabulary in the sentence never mattered.
items.grammar:
A/V-더니 reports something the speaker witnessed and then a change that followed. Two things go with it. The first clause is normally about someone or something other than the speaker — 내가 밥을 먹더니 is wrong — and the second clause is usually a contrast rather than a consequence.

The three it is set against are the three endings that look nearby and are not: -더라도 concedes a hypothetical (와도 in a stronger form), -아/어 가지고 is -아/어서 as people say it out loud, and -는 대신에 substitutes.

개다 is the weather verb for clearing after rain, and 맑게 개다 is the set phrase. Note the written ending: 개었다, not 개었어요 — questions 1 and 2 of the paper are printed in the plain written style throughout.

items.phraseKo: 수민이는 "너무 피곤하니까 오늘은 일찍 집에 가서 (   )!" 하고 말했다.

lines.ko: 수민이는 "너무 피곤하니까 오늘은 일찍 집에 가서 {}!" 하고 말했다.

items.en: Sumin said, "I’m so tired — today I’ll go straight home and get some rest!" The ending has to be a resolution the speaker makes to herself.
items.why:
Read the frame before the gap. 수민이는 "…" 하고 말했다 is direct quotation: everything between the marks is Sumin speaking, so the "I" inside is Sumin. That one fact removes two of the four options before you weigh their meanings, because two of these endings are restricted by person.

-더라 reports what you witnessed of somebody else. 쉬더라 is "(I saw that) they rested". Korean will not let you use it of your own resting, and inside this quotation the rester is the speaker.

-(으)ㄹ걸 has two lives and neither fits. As regret it looks back at what you did not do — I should have rested — while 오늘은 … 가서 is a plan for a day that has not finished. As conjecture it guesses about someone else, which the quotation again rules out.

-기도 하다 is the additive one: I also rest, I sometimes rest. But 오늘은 carries 은, setting today against other days, and the sentence ends in an exclamation mark. Both are asking for a decision, and a habit is not a decision.

Which leaves 3. -아/어야지 is the ending Korean uses to tell yourself what you are going to do. Everything in the sentence has been building to it: 너무 피곤하니까 gives the reason, 오늘은 marks the break from routine, and the exclamation mark is the resolve landing.

Worth noticing that the same habit settled both questions of this type. Question 1 turned on two time words; this one turns on who is speaking. Neither needed the vocabulary.
items.grammar:
-아/어야지 is a resolution spoken to oneself: 이제 자야지, 나도 운동해야지. Said to someone else with the right intonation it becomes a nudge — 빨리 자야지 — but the first-person use is what the exam tests.

The three it is set against are all person-restricted or aspect-restricted. -더라 needs a subject other than the speaker and something the speaker saw. -(으)ㄹ걸 is regret (안 갈걸 그랬다) or supposition (지금쯤 도착했을걸). -기도 하다 adds an occasional or additional case.

쉬다 is to rest, and 피곤하다 is to be tired — the two words the sentence is built out of. 하고 말했다 is direct quotation, keeping the words as spoken; 라고 is the other direct marker, and indirect speech would be -다고 or -냐고.

One more thing the sentence is quietly teaching: it uses -(으)니까 for the reason rather than -아/어서. That is the rule — when what follows is a suggestion, a command or a resolve, Korean wants -(으)니까. 피곤해서 쉬어야지 is the version that sounds wrong to a native ear.

items.phraseKo: 비장애인도 쉽지 (   ) 불편한 몸으로 높은 산에 오르다니 정말 대단한 사람이다.

lines.ko: 비장애인도 쉽지 {} 불편한 몸으로 높은 산에 오르다니 정말 대단한 사람이다.

items.en: It would hardly be easy even for someone without a disability — and to climb a high mountain with a body that struggles! A truly remarkable person.
items.why:
The sentence ends in admiration: 오르다니 정말 대단한 사람이다. -다니 is the ending for being struck by something, so whatever fills the blank has to set that up.

What sets admiration up is a contrast, and the sentence has already built one: 비장애인도, with 도 meaning even — even someone who has no disability. The half before the blank is saying the climb is hard for anybody; the half after is saying this person did it anyway.

-(으)ㄹ 텐데 is exactly that shape. It supposes — it would surely not be easy — and the 데 leaves the sentence hanging on a but. Nothing else in the list does both.

-(으)ㄹ까 봐 is worry: 쉽지 않을까 봐 means fearing it might not be easy, and it needs a second clause where somebody takes a precaution. Admiring a stranger is not a precaution.

-(으)ㄹ 테니까 supposes and then gives an instruction: 쉽지 않을 테니까 준비를 잘 하세요. The second half here is an exclamation, and you cannot base a command on it.

-(으)ㄴ 데다가 adds a second drawback to the first. It would need what follows to be another difficulty, and what follows is the achievement.

So the four are a contrast, a worry, a reason for an instruction and an addition. Only the contrast can carry a 다니.
items.grammar:
-(으)ㄹ 텐데 is 터 (a supposition) plus -인데, and the 데 is what makes it lean forward: 비가 올 텐데 우산을 안 가져갔어요. Notice that it is built from the same 터 as -(으)ㄹ 테니까 — the difference is entirely in what comes after, a contrast against a reason.

-다니 expresses being struck by something, and it takes the plain form: 오르다니, 먹다니, 그렇게 빠르다니. It almost always wants a contrast in front of it, which is why this question can be answered from the ending alone.

비장애인 is 비- (non-) plus 장애인, the same prefix as 비공개, 비무장. And 도 here is even, not also — 비장애인도 쉽지 않다 means it is not easy even for them.

items.phraseKo: 앞으로 날씨가 따뜻해지면서 산이 점점 푸르게 (   ).

lines.ko: 앞으로 날씨가 따뜻해지면서 산이 점점 푸르게 {}.

items.en: As the weather warms from now on, the mountains will gradually turn green. The ending has to carry a change moving away from now.
items.why:
All four are 변하다 with a different helping verb behind it, and two of them are a genuine pair worth learning together.

-아/어 가다 and -아/어 오다 both describe a change in progress, and they differ only in direction. 가다 runs away from now into the future; 오다 runs from the past up to now. 살아 왔다 is the life you have lived so far; 살아 갈 것이다 is the life ahead.

The sentence settles it in its first word. 앞으로 means from now on, and 점점 says the change is gradual rather than done. A gradual change pointed at the future is -아/어 가다, and 올 것이다 would have the greening arrive from the past, which 앞으로 has just ruled out.

-아/어 보다 is to try doing something, and trying needs somebody who decides to try. A mountain does not attempt to be green.

-아/어 대다 is to keep on doing something more than one would like, and it is used of people and usually with disapproval — 떠들어 대다, 먹어 대다. Neither the subject nor the tone fits.

Worth noticing what decided it: one adverb. The vocabulary of the sentence never came into it, which is what this question type does.
items.grammar:
변하다 is to change into something else. Behind it, -아/어 가다 and -아/어 오다 are the aspectual pair for a change under way, and the arrow is the whole difference: 가다 forward from now, 오다 backward to now.

-아/어 보다 (try) and -아/어 대다 (keep on, excessively) are the other two helping verbs learners meet at the same time. 대다 carries disapproval and needs a human subject, which is why it can be ruled out without reading the rest.

따뜻해지면서 is three pieces: 따뜻하다, the change ending -아/어지다 from Unit 15, and -(으)면서, which runs two things alongside each other. 푸르게 is 푸르다 in its adverbial form, describing how the mountain changes.

items.phraseKo: 올해는 과일 생산량이 (   ) 대체적으로 과일 가격이 내렸다.

lines.ko: 올해는 과일 생산량이 {} 대체적으로 과일 가격이 내렸다.

items.en: Perhaps because fruit output was up this year, fruit prices have generally come down. The ending has to offer a cause, and offer it tentatively.
items.why:
Look at the half after the blank before the options. 내렸다 is finished and past, and 대체적으로 hedges it — broadly speaking, on the whole. Something that has already happened, reported with a hedge, is waiting for a reason that is also hedged.

-아/어서인지 is exactly that: -아/어서 gives the cause, and -인지 admits the speaker is guessing. Perhaps because output rose. It is the only one of the four that offers a reason at all.

The other three are all about things that have not happened. -(ㄴ/는)다면 supposes — if output were to rise — and you cannot suppose your way to a price that has already fallen. -아/어야 sets a requirement, and requires a second clause that waits on it: 생산량이 늘어야 가격이 내린다, output has to rise for prices to fall. That is a rule, and this sentence is a report. -(ㄴ/는)다거나 offers one of several possibilities and needs the others named.

There is a spelling trap in two of them worth seeing. 늘다 is a ㄹ-stem, and the ㄹ drops before ㄴ, so 늘다 + -ㄴ다면 comes out 는다면 — the stem has vanished from the written form. Options 1 and 3 look as though they are missing their verb. They are not; the verb is the 느 you can no longer see.
items.grammar:
-아/어서인지 is three pieces: -아/어서 (because), 이다, and -(으)ㄴ지 (whether). Together they mean I am not certain, but perhaps because. Papers and reports like it because it lets them name a cause without claiming it.

The ㄹ-stem rule is what makes options 1 and 3 look strange. 늘다, 살다, 알다 and 만들다 all drop their ㄹ before ㄴ, ㅂ and ㅅ: 늘다 → 는다, 삽니다, 아세요, 만드는. Before a vowel the ㄹ stays, which is why options 2 and 4 keep 늘어-.

대체적으로 belongs to the same register as the sentence — written, careful, and unwilling to overstate. 생산량 is 생산 plus 량, the counter suffix for quantity: 강수량, 수출량, 통화량.

items.phraseKo: 의사는 위염 환자에게 식사량을 (   ).

lines.ko: 의사는 위염 환자에게 식사량을 {}.

items.en: The doctor had the gastritis patients cut down how much they ate. One particle in the sentence decides which ending can follow.
items.why:
The whole question is 에게, and it is worth circling. 에게 marks a person something is done to, and here that person is the patient. So the ending has to be one that can act on somebody — and only one of the four can.

-게 하다 is the causative: A makes B do it. 의사가 환자에게 조절하게 했다, the doctor had the patients regulate their intake. 에게 is exactly the marker it takes.

-게 되다 is its twin and its opposite. 하다 means somebody made it happen; 되다 means it came about with nobody making it. 환자가 조절하게 되었다 would be fine on its own — the patients came to cut down — but then the doctor has nothing to do and 에게 has no one to point at. This is the pair Unit 15 drills as V-게 되다, and the exam is checking you know the other half of it.

-(으)려고 fails for the same reason it failed in question 7 of the 유사 표현 set: the intender must be the doer. 의사가 조절하려고 했다 says the doctor intended to regulate — his own intake — and 환자에게 then has nowhere to attach. Twice now this ending has been the trap, and both times the tell was a second person in the sentence.

-ㄴ다고 한다 reports something at second hand: it is said that they regulate. A report is not an instruction, and again 에게 is left with no job.

One particle, four endings, and three of them have no use for it.
items.grammar:
조절하다 is to regulate or keep in check — 식사량을 조절하다, 온도를 조절하다.

-게 하다 and -게 되다 are the pair to hold side by side. -게 하다 needs an agent and marks the one made to act with 에게 or 을/를: 아이에게 약을 먹게 했다. -게 되다 has no agent at all: 약을 먹게 되었다, I ended up taking it. Unit 15 teaches the second; this question checks the first.

에게 is for people and animals; 에 is for places and things; 한테 is 에게 in speech. 환자에게 is the written one, which suits a sentence about a doctor.

식사량 is 식사 plus 량, the same quantity suffix as 생산량 in question 9.

items.phraseKo: 그의 행동을 보면 그는 (   ) 믿을 수가 없는 사람이다.

lines.ko: 그의 행동을 보면 그는 {} 믿을 수가 없는 사람이다.

items.en: Going by how he behaves, he is someone you could not trust however hard you tried.
items.why:
The half after the blank is 믿을 수가 없는, and that is the clue. One of the four options is not a free choice at all but the front half of a fixed pattern whose back half is already printed: -(으)려야 -(으)ㄹ 수 없다, try as you might to V, you cannot V. The same verb has to appear twice, and 믿- appears twice.

Once you see the pattern the question is over, because the other three would leave 믿을 수가 없는 with nothing to lean on.

믿어도 and 믿더라도 are both concessive — even if you believe. Put either in front of 믿을 수가 없다 and the sentence contradicts itself in the same breath: even if I believe, I cannot believe. Concession needs two different things.

믿는 통에 is a cause, and a specific kind: -는 통에 blames a mess. 아이가 우는 통에 아무것도 못 했다. Nothing here is chaotic, and a cause is not what the second half is waiting for.

This is the third question of this type to be settled by something outside the brackets — there the two time words, then 에게, and here the verb printed after the gap.
items.grammar:
-(으)려야 -(으)ㄹ 수 없다 is fixed and needs the same verb in both slots: 잊으려야 잊을 수 없다, 참으려야 참을 수 없다, 믿으려야 믿을 수 없다. It is a stronger 아무리 -아/어도 -(으)ㄹ 수 없다, and the doubling is what makes it recognisable on sight.

-는 통에 is worth keeping apart from the other causal endings this paper has used. -아/어서 is neutral, -(으)니까 leads to a decision, -(으)ㄴ 바람에 blames an unwelcome result, and -는 통에 blames a commotion.

수가 없다 is 수 없다 with 가 added for emphasis — the same 가 that turned up in -(으)ㄹ 수가 있다 in question 2 of this type.

items.phraseKo: 나를 간호해 주시는 어머니의 손에서 사랑이 (   ).

lines.ko: 나를 간호해 주시는 어머니의 손에서 사랑이 {}.

items.en: In the hands of the mother nursing me, love could be felt. One particle decides which of the four can stand.
items.why:
Look at 사랑이. The particle is 이, so 사랑 is the subject of whatever fills the blank — love is the thing doing, not the thing being done to. That rules out three of the four before their meanings matter.

느끼다 is the active verb and takes 을/를: 사랑을 느꼈다, I felt love. Every option except the first is built on it, so every one of them wants 사랑을 and gets 사랑이. 느껴 봤다 is trying to feel, 느끼는 듯했다 is seeming to feel, 느낄 정도였다 is to the extent of feeling — all three need a person as subject, and the person in this sentence is in 어머니의 손에서, marked as a place rather than an agent.

느껴지다 is the passive, and it takes 이/가: 사랑이 느껴졌다, love was felt. It is the only option that agrees with the particle already on the page.

Question 10 of this type turned on 에게 and this one turns on 이. Both are the same lesson: in Korean the particles are load-bearing, and an ending that disagrees with one is not a weaker answer but a broken sentence.
items.grammar:
느끼다 → 느껴지다 is the -아/어지다 passive, the same ending Unit 15 teaches as a change: 만들다 → 만들어지다, 보다 → 보여지다. With adjectives it makes a change; with transitive verbs it makes a passive.

The particle pair is the thing to hold: 사랑을 느끼다 against 사랑이 느껴지다. Swap the particle and you must swap the verb.

간호해 주시는 is three pieces — 간호하다, -아/어 주다 for doing it for someone, and -시- for the honorific, because it is 어머니. And 손에서 is 에서 marking where something comes from rather than who does it.

items.phraseKo: 노인 취업에 대한 설문 조사에서 건강이 (   ) 계속 일하고 싶다는 응답이 과반수를 넘었다.

lines.ko: 노인 취업에 대한 설문 조사에서 건강이 {} 계속 일하고 싶다는 응답이 과반수를 넘었다.

items.en: In a survey on employment among older people, more than half replied that they want to keep working for as long as their health allows.
items.why:
건강이 허락하는 한 is a set phrase: for as long as health permits. Learn it whole, because it turns up wherever anyone talks about working or travelling into old age.

The relation the sentence needs is a condition that has to keep holding. They want to go on working, and the working stops when the health does. -는 한 is the ending for exactly that: it holds while the condition holds.

Options 3 and 4 are both concessive, and they are concessive in the same direction. -(으)ㄹ지라도 and -ㄴ다고 해도 both mean even if health permits — which would say the wanting to work survives the health being fine. That is not a thought. Two options meaning the same thing is itself a signal: an exam does not offer two correct answers, so if you can see that a pair matches, both are wrong.

-길래 is a reason drawn from something observed, and it needs the speaker to do something about it: 날씨가 좋길래 산책했다. Here the second half is not something the speaker did; it is what a survey found.
items.grammar:
허락하다 is to permit. 건강이 허락하는 한, 시간이 허락하는 한 — the subject is the thing doing the permitting, which is why it is 건강이 and not 건강을.

-는 한 attaches to the present modifier and states a boundary: 내가 아는 한 (as far as I know), 특별한 일이 없는 한 (barring anything unusual).

-길래 is spoken and needs a first-person main clause with a completed action. -(으)ㄹ지라도 is the formal concessive, one step stiffer than -아/어도. -ㄴ/는다고 해도 concedes a supposition: even supposing that.

과반수 is 과 (exceeding) + 반수 (half the number), so 과반수를 넘었다 is strictly more than half of more than half — a doubling the papers use anyway. And N에 대한 modifies a noun (조사), where N에 대해서 would modify a verb.

exercises.pattern: 밑줄 친 부분과 의미가 비슷한 것 고르기
exercises.instructionKo: 다음 밑줄 친 부분과 의미가 비슷한 것을 고르십시오.
exercises.instructionEn: Choose the expression closest in meaning to the underlined part.
exercises.blurbEn: Four connectives on the same word, and only one of them names the same relation as the phrase underlined.
exercises.noteEn:
An underlined phrase, and four expressions to match it. The options always keep the same head word and change only what is attached to it, so vocabulary settles nothing — what is being tested is whether you can name the relation.

Sort the four by what they do before weighing any of them. A cause is not a correlation is not an addition is not a concession. A state left standing is not an obligation is not a habit is not a causative. An inevitability is not a permission is not an inference. Once they are sorted, the answer is whichever lands in the same box as the underlined phrase.

Expect the answer to be the stiffer of two synonyms. (으)로 인하여 pairs with (으)로 말미암아, -아/어 놓다 with -아/어 두다, -고자 with -기 위해서, -(으)ㄹ 따름이다 with -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다: in each pair the everyday form is underlined and the formal one is the answer, because that is the word the paper is checking you know.

Two things decide more of these than grammar does. The direction of time and of intent — you cannot enrol at a university and then travel there to do it. And whether the two clauses share a subject: -(으)려고 requires it, -도록 and V-게 do not, and a second person in the sentence removes an option before you have read it.

The same expression can be the trap in one question and the answer in the next. 가지고 is wrong where the sentence wants a contrast and right where it wants a sequence; 뿐 is wrong where the sentence wants a sequence and right where it wants a limit. Nothing about the word changes — what changes is the relation being asked for.

items.phraseKo: 취업 준비생의 70% 이상이 면접시험 준비를 할 때 외모로 인하여 고민해 본 적이 있다고 말했다.

lines.ko: 취업 준비생의 70% 이상이 면접시험 준비를 할 때 {} 고민해 본 적이 있다고 말했다.

items.en: Over 70% of job-seekers said they had worried about their looks when preparing for interviews. The underlined part states a cause, so its replacement must too.
items.why:
외모로 인하여 states a cause: because of appearance. Every option keeps 외모 and changes only what is attached to it, so the question is entirely about four connectives — and they are four different relations.

N에 따라서 is correlation. 외모에 따라서 결과가 다르다 means the outcome varies with appearance. Two things moving together is not one thing causing another, and the sentence is about what the worry came from.

N을/를 비롯해서 adds. It means including N, N first among them, and it is the same expression question 5 of the headline set turned on. Nothing in it explains anything.

N에도 불구하고 concedes, and it runs the opposite way: despite appearance. That would say the worrying happened even though looks were involved, which reverses the sentence.

That leaves 3. N(으)로 말미암아 is the formal twin of (으)로 인하여 — same meaning, same written register, and it is the answer precisely because it is the one of the four that nobody says casually. This question type rewards knowing the stiff written synonym rather than the everyday one.
items.grammar:
N(으)로 인하여 and N(으)로 인해(서) are one expression with two endings; 인하여 is the fuller written form, which is why it turns up in a report about a survey. N(으)로 말미암아 matches it in both meaning and register.

The three it is set against are the connectives learners meet at the same time and confuse: N에 따라서 (depending on — and note N에 따르면 is a different thing, according to a source), N을/를 비롯해서 (including), N에도 불구하고 (despite).

-아/어 보다 in 고민해 본 적이 있다 is the try-doing form, and -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다 is to have ever done it. Stacked, 고민해 본 적이 있다 = have had occasion to worry about it. Then -다고 말했다 reports it at second hand.

items.phraseKo: 시험 기간 동안 공부하는 학생이 많아서 도서관에 밤새도록 불을 켜 놓았다.

lines.ko: 시험 기간 동안 공부하는 학생이 많아서 도서관에 밤새도록 불을 {}.

items.en: So many students were studying during the exam period that the library left its lights on all night. The underlined part is a state left standing.
items.why:
불을 켜 놓았다 is not simply that the light went on. -아/어 놓다 says: do it, and leave the result standing. The light was switched on and stayed on, which is what 밤새도록 is there to tell you.

-아/어 두다 is its twin. Both mean do it and leave it, and they are near enough interchangeable that the difference is a matter of feel: 놓다 leans towards something you will come back to soon, 두다 towards something left for longer. Either fits a library at night, and that is why 4 is the answer.

The other three are three different things and none of them is a state. -아/어야 했다 is obligation, and nobody in the sentence was obliged to do anything. -곤 했다 is a habit repeated over time, but the sentence describes one exam period, not a recurring one. -게 했다 is causative — it would need somebody being made to switch the light on, and there is no such person here.

Four endings on 켜다, four grammatical categories: state, obligation, habit, cause. That is the shape of this question type, and it is the same shape as question 2 of the blank-filling set.
items.grammar:
-아/어 놓다 and -아/어 두다 are the resultative pair: 창문을 열어 놓다 (open the window and leave it open), 표를 미리 사 두다 (buy the ticket and have it ready). Without them, 불을 켰다 would only say the switch was flipped.

-곤 하다 is the repeated past: 주말이면 등산을 하곤 했다. -게 하다 is the causative, which has now appeared three times in this paper — 시원하게 해 주다 in question 7 of the headline set is the same ending.

밤새도록 is 밤새다 with -도록, which sets a limit: until the night is through. And 많아서 is -아/어서 giving the reason, the ending question 2 of the blank set had to be told apart from -(으)니까.

items.phraseKo: 친구가 입사 시험에 합격하도록 엿과 떡을 선물로 주었다.

lines.ko: 친구가 입사 시험에 {} 엿과 떡을 선물로 주었다.

items.en: I gave my friend yeot and tteok so that he would pass the company entrance exam. The underlined part is a purpose, and its replacement has to be one too.
items.why:
Two people are doing two different things in this sentence, and that is what decides it. The friend is the one who passes; the speaker is the one who gives the sweets. Once you have noticed that, one option is simply ungrammatical rather than merely wrong.

-(으)려고 is the trap, and it is a good one, because in English "in order to pass" sounds exactly right. Korean does not allow it: -(으)려고 requires the intender and the doer to be the same person. 내가 합격하려고 공부했다 is fine — I studied, I intended to pass. 친구가 합격하려고 내가 떡을 주었다 is not a sentence.

-도록 has no such restriction, which is exactly why the sentence uses it, and V-게 is its everyday twin. 아이가 잘 자도록 불을 껐다 and 아이가 잘 자게 불을 껐다 are the same sentence in two registers. That is the answer.

-거든 is a condition: if he passes. That would make the sweets a reward afterwards rather than a wish beforehand, and the tense would have to change with it.

-(으)ㄹ 만큼 is degree: enough to pass. It would say the sweets were sufficient in quantity to constitute passing, which is not a thought anyone has had.

So the four are a purpose, a condition, a same-subject intention and a degree — and the sentence has two subjects, which removes the intention before you weigh anything else.
items.grammar:
합격하다 is to pass an exam — the one thing every option in the list agrees on. -도록 and V-게 both mean so that, and neither cares whether the two clauses share a subject. -(으)려고 does care, and that single restriction is the whole of this question. It is worth memorising as a pair of sentences rather than as a rule: 친구가 합격하도록 떡을 주었다 (fine) against 친구가 합격하려고 떡을 주었다 (not a sentence).

-도록 has other senses the exam also uses — 밤새도록 in question 4 of this same type is the "until, to the extent of" one. Purpose and extent are the two, and which one is meant is decided by what the clause is about.

The sweets are not random. 엿 and 떡 are sticky, and 붙다 means both to stick and to pass an exam, so sticky food is what Korea gives a candidate. The opposite superstition runs alongside it: you do not eat 미역국 the morning of a test, because seaweed soup is slippery.

items.phraseKo: 한 나라의 미래는 그 나라의 교육 정책에 따라 달라진다.

lines.ko: 한 나라의 미래는 그 나라의 {}.

items.en: A country's future varies with its education policy. The underlined part says one thing depends on another, and so must its replacement.
items.why:
N에 따라 달라지다 says two things move together: change the policy and the future changes with it. N에 달려 있다 says the same thing in four words — it hangs on the policy. That is the answer, and the two are close enough that Korean uses them interchangeably in exactly this kind of sentence.

Options 1 and 2 both say the future *is* the policy rather than *depends on* it, which is a different relation altogether — and option 1 adds a past tense to a sentence that is a general truth in the present. 되었다 against 달라진다 is enough on its own.

Option 4 is the one worth slowing down for. (으)로 인한 것이다 states a cause, and a cause is not the same as a variable. 달라진다 says different policies give different futures; (으)로 인한 것이다 says the future that exists was produced by the policy. The first is a rule about how two things vary, the second is a claim about one outcome that has already happened.

There is a nice trap in that. (으)로 인하여 was the phrase question 3 of this same type was built on, where its twin (으)로 말미암아 was the answer. Here the same expression is the distractor. What a question asks you to match is never the word on its own — it is the relation the word names in that sentence.
items.grammar:
교육 is education and 정책 is a policy, so 교육 정책 is two ordinary words rather than one hard one — the same build as 부동산 정책 in question 7 of the headline set.

N에 따라 달라지다 and N에 달려 있다 are the pair to learn together: 성적은 노력에 따라 달라진다 = 성적은 노력에 달려 있다. 달려 있다 comes from 달리다, to hang, and the picture holds — the outcome hangs on the thing named.

N에 따라 and N에 따라서 are the same expression; the 서 is optional. Do not confuse either with N에 따르면, which reports a source: 신문에 따르면.

-일 수가 있다 in option 2 is -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 with 가 added for emphasis, and it attaches to a noun here through 이다: 정책 + 이 + ㄹ 수가 있다 → 정책일 수가 있다.

달라지다 is 다르다 with the change ending -아/어지다 — the same ending Unit 15 drills. To be different, and then to become different.

items.phraseKo: 꽃병에 개나리 꽃을 꽂아다가 책상 위에 놓으니 봄이 온 것 같다.

lines.ko: 꽃병에 개나리 꽃을 {} 책상 위에 놓으니 봄이 온 것 같다.

items.en: I stood forsythia in a vase and set it on the desk, and it feels as though spring has come. The underlined part is a sequence, and so must its replacement be.
items.why:
-아/어다가 does one thing and then carries the result somewhere to do the next: put the flowers in the vase, then take the vase to the desk. Two actions in order, with a move between them.

-아/어 가지고 is the spoken form of -아/어서, and -아/어서 is the plain sequence: do this, then that. It is the only option in the list that puts two actions in order at all, which is why it is the answer even though it says nothing about carrying.

The other three are all about why or how much. -(으)ㄹ 뿐 limits: only stood them in, and nothing else — which contradicts the desk. -았/었기에 is a formal cause, and the flowers being in the vase is not the reason the desk got them. -(으)ㄴ 바람에 is also a cause, and specifically one whose result nobody wanted: 버스를 놓친 바람에 지각했다. Spring arriving is not a misfortune.

Worth noticing where you have seen 가지고 before. It was option 3 in question 1 of the 빈칸 set — 와 가지고 — and there it was wrong, because that sentence needed a contrast and 가지고 gives a sequence. Same ending, opposite verdict, and the difference is the relation the sentence is asking for.
items.grammar:
-아/어다가 needs the object to move: 도서관에서 책을 빌려다가 읽었어요, 시장에서 생선을 사다가 구웠어요. Borrow it, bring it, read it. Drop the carrying and it becomes plain -아/어서.

-아/어 가지고 is 가지다 worn down into an ending, and it is everyday speech for -아/어서. Both a sequence and a cause, decided by context.

꽂다 is to stand something upright into something else — 꽃을 꽂다, 이어폰을 꽂다, 콘센트에 꽂다. And 놓으니 is -(으)니, which links an action to what you then notice: put it down, and spring seemed to have arrived.

items.phraseKo: 정부의 노력에도 불구하고 국가의 경제 상황이 나아지지 않는 것이 안타까울 따름이다.

lines.ko: 정부의 노력에도 불구하고 국가의 경제 상황이 나아지지 않는 것이 {}.

items.en: Despite the government’s efforts, that the country’s economy is not improving is simply a shame. The underlined part is a limit — only this, nothing more.
items.why:
-(으)ㄹ 따름이다 and -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 are the same expression in two registers. Both mean: it is only this and there is nothing else to say. 따름 is the stiffer of the two, which is why the written sentence uses it and why the exam asks for the everyday one.

The other three are three different modal claims and none of them is a limit. -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 says it might be a shame, leaving the door open. -(으)ㄹ 정도이다 measures: to such an extent that it is a shame, which would need something being measured. -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 denies outright: there is no way it could be a shame, which reverses the sentence.

And 뿐 is worth looking at twice. It was option 1 in question 11, where it was wrong; here it is the answer. Nothing about the word changed — what changed is that question 11 wanted a sequence and this one wants a limit. That is the whole lesson of this question type in two consecutive questions.
items.grammar:
-(으)ㄹ 따름이다 = -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 = only this, nothing further. Both attach to the future modifier: 감사할 따름이다, 부끄러울 뿐이다.

Note that 뿐 has two lives. After a modifier it is this limiting one; after a noun it means only that noun — 너뿐이야. And in question 11 it appeared as -(으)ㄹ 뿐 without 이다, which limits an action rather than closing a sentence.

N에도 불구하고 is the concessive from question 3 of this type, here doing its proper job at last. 나아지다 is 낫다 with the change ending -아/어지다 — to be better, then to get better — and 안타깝다 is the ㅂ-irregular, giving 안타까울.

items.phraseKo: 한국의 대학교에 입학하고자 한국으로 오는 유학생들이 날로 증가하고 있다.

lines.ko: 한국의 대학교에 {} 한국으로 오는 유학생들이 날로 증가하고 있다.

items.en: The number of international students coming to Korea in order to enter a Korean university is rising by the day. The underlined part is a purpose.
items.why:
-고자 states a purpose in the written register: they come in order to enrol. Its everyday twin is -기 위해서, and that is the answer — the same swap this question type keeps asking for, where the stiff form is underlined and the plain one is what you must recognise.

The other three are all about time or futility, and none of them is a reason for coming.

-고서 is sequence: enrol first, then come. That reverses the order of events, because you cannot enrol at a Korean university and then travel to Korea to do it.

-자마자 is immediacy: the moment they enrol, they come. Same problem, tighter timing.

-아/어 봤자 concedes and then dismisses: even if they get in, it is no use. That is not why anybody buys a plane ticket, and the second half of the sentence — numbers rising by the day — says the opposite.

Worth noticing that the sentence would still read smoothly with any of them. What rules out three is not grammar but the direction of time and of intent, which is the same test question 11 of this type set with 꽂아다가.
items.grammar:
입학하다 is to be admitted to a school, and it takes 에: 대학교에 입학하다. 졸업하다 takes 를. -고자 belongs to writing and speeches: 말씀드리고자 합니다, 알아보고자 한다. In speech people say -(으)려고 or -기 위해서 instead. All three are purpose, and -(으)려고 is the one with the same-subject restriction that decided question 7 and question 10 — -고자 and -기 위해서 share it, which is why they can stand in for each other here.

-고서 is -고 with 서 pinning the order down, so it is sequence and never cause. -자마자 is tighter still: no gap at all between the two.

-아/어 봤자 is 보다 turned into a dismissal: 아무리 -아/어 봤자 소용없다. It always expects a negative outcome behind it.

날로 is day by day and goes with a verb of increase: 날로 증가하다, 날로 발전하다. 증가하다 is the formal counterpart of 늘다 from the 어휘 pages.

items.phraseKo: 무슨 일이든 처음 시작할 때는 힘든 법이다.

lines.ko: 무슨 일이든 처음 시작할 때는 {}.

items.en: Whatever the task, the beginning is bound to be hard. The underlined part states an inevitability, not an observation.
items.why:
-(으)ㄴ/는 법이다 says: that is how things are and could not be otherwise. It is a statement about the nature of the thing, which is why 무슨 일이든 — whatever the task — is standing in front of it. The sentence is a general truth, not a report about one job.

-기 마련이다 means exactly that and is the answer. The two are close enough that Korean teaching materials introduce them on the same page.

The other three are three different things, and each of them narrows the sentence from a truth to a case.

-아/어도 되다 is permission: it is all right for it to be hard. That says somebody is allowed something, and nobody is asking permission here.

-기만 하다 is exclusivity: it does nothing but be hard. That is a complaint about one job rather than a rule about all of them, and 무슨 일이든 has already said all of them.

-(으)ㄴ 모양이다 is inference from evidence: it looks as though it is hard. An inference is drawn from something in front of you, and a general truth has nothing in front of it to look at.

Sorting them by what they do is the whole method of this type: inevitability, permission, exclusivity, inference — and the underlined phrase is the first.
items.grammar:
-(으)ㄴ/는 법이다 and -기 마련이다 are the pair to learn together: 노력하면 성공하는 법이다 = 노력하면 성공하기 마련이다. 법이다 takes the modifier (힘든, 하는), 마련이다 takes -기 (힘들기, 하기), which is the only thing to keep straight when swapping one for the other.

-(으)ㄴ 모양이다 is worth separating from both. It is inference, so it needs evidence: 불이 꺼진 걸 보니 잔 모양이다. That is why it cannot state a truth about every task.

힘들다 is a ㄹ-stem: 힘든 before ㄴ with the ㄹ dropped, 힘들기 before -기 with it kept. Both appear in this question, which is a fair test on its own — the same rule that made 늘다 come out 는다면 in question 9 of the 빈칸 set.

exercises.instructionKo: 다음 글 또는 도표의 내용과 같은 것을 고르십시오.
exercises.instructionEn: Choose the statement that agrees with the notice.
exercises.blurbEn: A poster with its four labelled lines, and four statements — three of which change one detail the poster had already settled.
exercises.noteEn:
A notice — a poster, a leaflet, a chart — and four statements about it. One of them survives a check against the page and the other three each change exactly one thing the notice had already settled.

So this is a checking job rather than a reading one, and it goes faster done backwards. Take a statement, find the single line of the notice it is about, and compare those two only. A poster prints four or five labelled lines and the four options divide them up between themselves, so nearly every option is settled by one line and nothing else on the page matters to it.

Four places the change is usually made.

1. The wrong date range. An event notice prints two of them — the window for applying and the stretch the thing actually runs — and the option quotes one while asking about the other. Count the named months of the second range on your fingers; the arithmetic between the two dates is not what is being asked.

2. The channel swapped. Apply on the website becomes apply in person, or the other way round. A notice names one way of applying and only one, so 직접 or 홈페이지 in an option is a word to go straight back to the 신청 방법 line with.

3. Eligibility widened out of its category. A bracketed also-eligible extends a list without leaving it: 고등학생 또는 대학생, and then foreign students who speak Korean — still students. The option that turns that into anybody has crossed a line the bracket did not cross.

4. The title said again in easier words. 모집 becomes 찾고 있다, 어린이 becomes 아이, 그림책 becomes 책. Nothing added and nothing dropped — which is what a correct option looks like on this type, and why it reads as too obvious to be the answer.

The habit worth building is to read the labels down the left of the notice before reading a single option — 자격, 모집 기간, 신청 방법, 활동 기간. Those labels are the four things that can be asked about, and knowing them in advance turns each option into one lookup.

items.en: Volunteers wanted to read picture books aloud. "Give children a dream and a hope." Eligible: high school or university students (a foreign student with good Korean is eligible too). Applications 10–21 November, through the Inju Children’s Library website. The work runs 1 December 2025 to 28 February 2026.
items.why:
The title is the answer, in easier words. 그림책 읽어 주는 자원봉사자 모집 is a call for volunteers who read picture books aloud, and option 2 says the same thing with everyday vocabulary: 모집 becomes 찾고 있다, 어린이 becomes 아이, 그림책 becomes 책, and 읽어 주는 becomes 읽어 줄. Nothing has been added and nothing dropped, which is the shape a correct option takes on this type.

Option 1 counts the wrong range, and then counts it wrong. The poster prints two date ranges and only the second one is the volunteering: 활동 기간 runs 2025년 12월 1일 to 2026년 2월 28일, which is December, January and February — three months. The 모집 기간 above it is eleven days. Neither range is two months, so the number in the option is not on the page at all.

Option 3 swaps the channel. 신청 방법 names one way to apply and it is a web address, so 도서관에 직접 가서 해야 한다 is the opposite of what the line says. 직접 is the tell — the moment an option says in person, go back to the 신청 방법 line and read it again.

Option 4 widens the eligibility out of its own category. 자격 says 고등학생 또는 대학생, and the bracket after it adds foreign students who speak Korean well. That extends the list without leaving it: every person the bracket lets in is still 학생. 학생이 아닌 사람들 is exactly who the 자격 line rules out, and a bracketed exception on this type is almost always an extension rather than an exit.

Read in the other order — labels first, options second — three of the four are settled by one line each: 활동 기간 kills option 1, 신청 방법 kills option 3, 자격 kills option 4. The one left is checked against the title, and it matches.
items.grammar:
읽어 주는 is 읽다 plus -아/어 주다, which is doing something for somebody else rather than for yourself. 그림책을 읽다 is reading a picture book; 그림책을 읽어 주다 is reading one to someone. The whole notice rests on that 주다 — without it the volunteers would be reading to themselves. 읽어 주는 is the present modifier (the volunteer who reads) and 읽어 줄 the future one (the volunteer who will read), and the option swapping one for the other changes nothing.

어린이 and 아이 are the same person in two registers. 어린이 is the word institutions and notices use — 어린이집, 어린이날, and the 인주어린이도서관 on this poster — and 아이 is what anyone says out loud. Recognising that they refer to the same children is half of what this question tests.

또는 joins two nouns in written Korean where speech would use 이나: 고등학생 또는 대학생 is 고등학생이나 대학생. It belongs with 및 and 등 as notice vocabulary rather than conversation.

선물하다 is 선물 turned into a verb, and 꿈과 희망을 선물하다 is a fixed piece of poster Korean — you give someone a dream and a hope. The imperative 선물하세요 is aimed at the reader, which is why a recruitment poster addresses the volunteer rather than the children.

도 in 외국인 학생도 가능 adds to a list that has already been given; it never replaces it. That is the particle deciding option 4, and it is the same 도 in 사람들도 — which is the option trying to add a group the 자격 line never opened.

items.phraseKo: 여행사를 선택할 때 중요하게 생각하는 것

lines.ko: 여행사를 선택할 때 중요하게 생각하는 것
성인 남녀 1,600명

choices.ko: 회사의 규모가 중요하다고 응답한 비율이 가장 낮다.
가격을 중요하게 생각하는 사람이 전체의 반을 넘는다.
이용 후기가 여행 상품의 다양성보다 중요하다는 응답이 두 배 이상 많다.
여행 상품의 다양성보다 회사의 규모를 중요하게 생각하는 사람이 더 적다.

items.en: What people weigh when choosing a travel agency. Price 48%, the range of travel packages 25%, the size of the company 16%, customer reviews 9%, other 2%. (Surveyed: 1,600 adult men and women.)
items.why:
A chart question is a comparison, not a calculation. Every option names two slices and says something about the pair, so the work is to find which two and then read only those. Option 4 names 여행 상품의 다양성 at 25% and 회사의 규모 at 16%, and 16 is the smaller of the two — which is exactly what it claims. Nothing else on the chart bears on it.

Option 1 fails on 가장. 회사의 규모 is 16%, the third of five slices: 기타 sits at 2% and 이용 후기 at 9%, both below it. 가장 is a claim about every other slice at once, so a single smaller one settles it, and a chart of five will usually print two below whatever the option picks.

Option 2 fails by two points. 전체의 반 is 50% and 가격 is 48%, and 반을 넘는다 needs more than half rather than nearly half. A number just short of a round threshold is a shape this type keeps using: 48, 49, 33 against a third. Read the threshold before the slice.

Option 3 has the two sides the wrong way round. 이용 후기 is 9% and 여행 상품의 다양성 is 25%, so the bigger of that pair is 다양성, and it is 다양성 that is nearly three times 후기 rather than the reverse. 두 배 이상 is doing work of its own: it survives only if the ratio reaches two, and 9 to 25 is 2.8 in the other direction. A comparison that still reads well with its two nouns exchanged is worth checking in both directions before it is believed.

The habit for this type is to read the option backwards — verb first. 가장 낮다, 반을 넘는다, 두 배 이상 많다, 더 적다 each ask for a different pair of numbers, and naming the pair first turns four options into four lookups. Three of these are settled without ever reading the fourth slice.
items.grammar:
보다 attaches to the thing being compared against, and the sentence then says something about the other one. 여행 상품의 다양성보다 회사의 규모를 … 더 적다 makes 다양성 the standard and 규모 the thing measured, so 규모 is what comes out smaller. Exchange the two nouns and the sentence still reads perfectly while claiming the opposite — which is the whole of option 3.

중요하다 turns up in three shapes here and the ending says what each clause is doing. 중요하게 is the adverb on 생각하다: 중요하게 생각하다 is to regard something as important, and it is the standard way a survey question is worded. 중요하다고 is the quoted form under 응답하다. 중요하다는 is that same quotation turned into a modifier, so 중요하다는 응답 is a response to the effect that it matters.

가장 is the superlative and it goes in front of the adjective: 가장 낮다, 가장 많다. It claims about the whole set at once, which is why it is the easiest word on a chart question to disprove.

전체의 반 is half of the whole, and 반을 넘다 is to pass it. The noun for the same idea is 과반수, which the 빈칸 set already used as 과반수를 넘었다 — 과 exceeding plus 반수 half the number, so it says twice over what 반을 넘다 says once.

Every label on this chart is N의 N: 회사의 규모, 여행 상품의 다양성, and that is how a survey names a criterion rather than a thing. 기타 closes almost every Korean chart. It is not a word anyone says out loud; it means everything that did not earn a slice of its own. The 설문 대상 line under the chart names who was asked — 성인 남녀 1,600명 — and it is what turns a percentage into a number of people. Three of these four options talk about 사람 or 응답 rather than 비율, and that line is what licenses them to.
